summary: Defines the Target-Dialog header field and the tdialog option tag for the Session Initiation Protocol. A request that creates a SIP dialog can use it to tell the recipient that the sender knows about an existing dialog with it. The recipient can use this to decide whether to authorize the request. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: In the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), a program sometimes needs to prove that it already knows about an ongoing call before the other side will accept its request. RFC 4538 adds a Target-Dialog header field that names an existing call by its identifiers, so the recipient can check the claim and authorize the request. This makes out-of-dialog requests such as call transfers safer and easier to handle.

subtitle: A SIP header that lets a request prove the sender knows about an existing dialog, so it can be authorized.

tldr.problem: A SIP user agent often must decide whether to accept a new dialog-creating request, such as a REFER for a call transfer, and the right answer can depend on whether the sender knows about an existing dialog with it.
tldr.mechanism: The sender adds a Target-Dialog header field carrying the Call-ID, local tag and remote tag of that dialog, and the tdialog option tag signals support. The recipient checks the identifiers against its dialog.
tldr.outcome: The recipient can authorize the request outside the dialog without the problems of reusing the dialog. Security depends on the dialog using a sips URI and on cryptographically random identifiers.

today: RFC 4538 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the SIP core specification, RFC 3261.

sections.title: Why Dialog Awareness Matters
sections.content:
A SIP dialog is a persistent relationship between a pair of user agents, created by requests such as INVITE, REFER and SUBSCRIBE. A user agent that receives a dialog-creating request must decide whether to authorize it. In many situations that decision depends on whether the sender is currently in a dialog with the user agent, or is aware of a dialog the user agent has with another entity.

The RFC gives three examples. In call transfer, user agent A sends a REFER to B asking B to call C; B should accept it if B has an INVITE dialog with A. Current implementations send the REFER inside that same dialog, which causes problems determining the dialog's lifecycle and which messages belong to which application usage. Sending the REFER outside the dialog is better, but then B needs a way to authorize it.

In the application interaction framework, a proxy on the path of an INVITE sends a REFER to a user agent's Globally Routable User Agent URI (GRUU), asking it to fetch a user interface component. And an element on the INVITE path may send a SUBSCRIBE for the dialog event package to track the state of the INVITE. In both cases the request should be authorized if it comes from an entity that was on the path of the original dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP programs keep a shared context, called a dialog, for each ongoing call. Sometimes a program should only accept a new request if the sender already knows about that context. This RFC defines a way for the sender to prove it.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
User agent A sends an INVITE to user agent B through two servers acting as proxies. User B answers with a 200 OK whose Supported header field includes the tdialog option tag, and the dialog is established.

Later, an entity that was present along the request path, such as server A, wishes to send a dialog-forming request like a REFER to user agent B. It acts as a user agent and addresses the request to the URI it learned from the Contact header field of the 200 OK. If that URI has the GRUU property, the mechanism works across NAT boundaries. The request contains a Target-Dialog header field with the dialog identifiers of the INVITE dialog: the Call-ID, the local tag and the remote tag. The sender knew to include it because it knows that user agent B supports the extension.

When the request arrives, user agent B makes its authorization decision. Because the INVITE dialog was established using a sips URI and the dialog identifiers are cryptographically random, no entity except user agent B, user agent A, or the proxies on the initial INVITE path can know those identifiers. So because the request carries them, user agent B can be certain the request came from one of those entities, or from an entity to which they gave the identifiers, and it authorizes the request.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who took part in the original call knows its three identifiers. A later request that quotes those identifiers can only have come from a participant. The recipient checks the identifiers and, if they match, treats the sender as a participant.

sections.title: When the Sender Includes the Header
sections.content:
A user agent client SHOULD include a Target-Dialog header field in a request when all four conditions hold: the request is to be sent outside any existing dialog; the client believes the server may not authorize the request unless the client can prove awareness of the dialog identifiers of some other dialog (the target dialog); the request does not already contain that proof; and the client knows the server supports the header field, which it can know from a Supported header field with the tdialog option tag seen inside the target dialog. If the fourth condition is not met, the client SHOULD NOT use this specification and instead SHOULD send the request within the existing target dialog if it can.

The callid value MUST equal the Call-ID of the target dialog. The remote-tag parameter MUST be present and hold the tag that the recipient of the new request views as remote; the local-tag parameter MUST be present and hold the tag the recipient views as local.

The request SHOULD also include a Require header field with the tdialog option tag. In principle it should never fail with a 420 (Bad Extension) response, because the client only sends it when it believes the server supports the extension. The Require header lets the client tell two 403 responses apart: one where the server did not understand Target-Dialog, in which case the client should retry inside the target dialog, and one where the server understood it but still refused, in which case the client should not retry inside the dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender quotes the identifiers only when a request goes outside the call, the receiver may need the proof, no other part of the request carries it, and the receiver has said it understands this header. Sending the option tag in Require lets the sender tell a refusal apart from simple confusion.

sections.title: Server Behavior and Proxies
sections.content:
A user agent server that receives a dialog-creating request and wishes to authorize it, where that authorization depends on whether the sender has knowledge of an existing dialog and nothing outside the header field proves it, SHOULD check the request for the Target-Dialog header field. If the field is absent, the server MAY still authorize the request by other means.

If the callid, remote-tag and local-tag values match the Call-ID, remote tag and local tag of an existing dialog, and that dialog was established using a sips URI, the server SHOULD authorize the request if it would authorize any entity on the path of the request that created that dialog, or any entity trusted by such an entity.

If the identifiers match a dialog that was not created with a sips URI, the server MAY authorize the request on the same basis, but authorization is optional: any eavesdropper on the original dialog path would have had access to the dialog identifiers. If the identifiers do not match, or either tag parameter is missing, the header field MUST be ignored and authorization MAY be determined by other means. Proxy behavior is unaffected by this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving program checks the quoted identifiers against its own dialogs. A match on a protected call is strong proof, so it should authorize; a match on an unprotected call is weaker, so it may authorize. Anything that does not match is ignored.

sections.title: Header Definition and Announcing Support
sections.content:
The Target-Dialog header field consists of the Call-ID followed by optional parameters remote-tag, local-tag and generic parameters. It is allowed in requests, with no action for proxies, and the RFC's method tables show it on INVITE, SUBSCRIBE and REFER. It has no compact form.

The mechanism depends on the client knowing, ahead of time, that the server supports the header field, and the client learns this from a Supported header field carrying the tdialog option tag. User agents implementing this RFC should therefore include a Supported header field in all dialog-forming requests and responses; RFC 3261 already makes that a SHOULD and this RFC does not change it. Unless the option tag appears in Supported, the extension is unlikely to be used and the request will probably be re-sent inside the existing dialog.

The RFC registers the header field, the two header field parameters local-tag and remote-tag with no predefined values under the process of RFC 3968, and the tdialog option tag. In a Require header the option tag means the recipient must support the extension; in a Supported header it means the sender supports it.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is a call identifier plus two tag values. Programs must announce in every call setup message that they understand the tdialog option, or other programs will not know it is safe to use the header.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The header field authorizes requests on the basis that the sender has access to information that only certain entities have. Two conditions make that decision secure. First, no eavesdropper may have access to the information, which requires the original SIP dialog to have been established using a sips URI, providing TLS on each hop; with a sips URI only the user agents and proxies on the request path can know the dialog identifiers.

Second, the dialog identifiers must be random enough that they cannot be guessed. RFC 3261 requires global uniqueness for the Call-ID and 32 bits of cryptographic randomness for each of the two tags. Given the short duration of a typical dialog, perhaps as long as a day, the RFC judges this adequate to prevent guessing attacks. It insists on true cryptographic randomness as set forth in RFC 4086: weaker pseudorandom identifiers reduce the chance of collision but are guessable, so an attacker could observe a sequence of identifiers, guess the next one, and use this specification to launch an attack.
sections.plainLanguage: The proof is only as good as the secrecy of the identifiers. The call must be encrypted hop by hop so nobody can listen in, and the identifiers must be truly random so nobody can guess them.

sections.title: Difference from In-Reply-To
sections.content:
RFC 3261 defines the In-Reply-To header field, which lists the Call-IDs of calls that the current request references, much like Reply-To in email, to help build conversation threads in a user interface. Both header fields reference a previous session, but they are not substitutes for each other.

  • In-Reply-To is meant for a human or a user interface widget, to give the user context for deciding what a call is about. Target-Dialog is meant for the user agent itself, to authorize requests where the decision belongs to the protocol rather than the user.
  • Target-Dialog references a specific dialog that must be currently in progress, which is why it uses a set of dialog identifiers. In-Reply-To references a previous call attempt, most likely one that produced no dialog, which is why it uses only a Call-ID.
  • In-Reply-To implies cause and effect: the request is sent because of the previous request. Target-Dialog implies no cause and effect, only awareness, for the purpose of authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: One header field is a note for a person about which earlier call this one relates to. The other is a check performed by the phone itself, and it points at a call that is still running.

messages.label: REFER
messages.note: Sent to A's GRUU; carries Target-Dialog and Require: tdialog.

messages.label: 200 OK
messages.note: Authorized because Target-Dialog matches the dialog.

data.title: Target-Dialog ABNF
data.code:
Target-Dialog      =     "Target-Dialog" HCOLON callid *(SEMI
                             td-param)    ;callid from RFC 3261
td-param           =     remote-param / local-param /
                         generic-param
remote-param       =     "remote-tag" EQUAL token
local-param        =     "local-tag" EQUAL token
                           ;token and generic-param from RFC 3261
